Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 75
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Sculptor
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 75

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Meaning Seeking: I think about why the event has happened to me, Body Monitoring: constantly check body for signs of danger or injury, Avoid Physical Stress: Situations that put my body under stress
  Negative Appraisals: Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened

Vignette:
Elias had been forty-eight when the studio’s support beam fractured without warning. He remembered the groan of stressed metal, the sudden tilt of the floor, and the weight of a half-finished marble plinth sliding toward him. There was a crunch, then the sensation of being pinned beneath cold stone and twisted rebar. For two hours, he waited in the dark, listening to his own ragged breathing while a fire extinguisher hissed nearby. When the rescue workers finally cut him free, he emerged with a collapsed lung, three cracked ribs, and a leg that would never fully straighten. In the weeks that followed, Elias stopped sleeping through the night. He constantly checked his body, pressing his thumbs against his ribs after breakfast and pausing on every step of his morning walk, waiting for a new twinge in his knee or a sudden tightness in his chest. He had come to believe he could no longer trust his own body, viewing it as an unreliable vessel that might fail without warning. What frightened him most was not pain itself, but the silence that preceded it—the absence of familiar signals that told him he was still intact. He found himself thinking about why the event had happened to him, turning the accident over and over in his mind. He was certain he had permanently changed for the worse, no longer the man who could command his physical space. He felt his body had been permanently damaged by what happened, a shift so fundamental that his hands, once steady enough to carve veining into wet clay, now felt foreign and prone to sudden tremors when he reached for tools. His daily routine settled around these realities. He avoided situations that put his body under stress, steering clear of uneven pavement, crowded galleries, and any environment requiring heavy lifting or climbing. He stopped entering the south side of his studio, where the heavy anvil and steel frames stood. When clients called to commission pieces, he politely declined. His studio, once a cavernous space echoing with the clink of chisels and the smell of mineral oil, grew quiet. He continued to work, but only from a low stool, carving smaller forms in soft wax that required minimal physical exertion. The accumulation of these adjustments was gradual. He no longer trusted his legs to carry him up the four steps to his second-floor apartment, so he moved his bed into the ground-floor room. The space felt less like a home and more like a station. At seventy-five, with his wife’s photograph resting on a shelf beside a box of untouched business cards, Elias finally sat down to make a call. The silence in the studio had become unbearable, not because of the work he missed, but because of the constant internal alarm he could no longer outrun. He wanted to understand whether the man he had been could ever return, or if he was simply meant to manage what remained. He was most afraid that his body would betray him completely, leaving him stranded without explanation, but he hoped, quietly, to stop scanning for danger long enough to breathe.
